claim: The latest Apache Kafka documentation at fetch time is for 4.3.X (4.2 docs are labelled an older version). Quotes below from the 4.3 design page.
quote: AK 4.3.X
notes: The 4.2 design page says: You are viewing documentation for an older version (4.2) of Kafka.

claim: Kafka's definitions of at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once.
quote:
At most once –Messages may be lost but are never redelivered.
At least once –Messages are never lost but may be redelivered.
Exactly once –Each message is processed once and only once.
notes: Section Message Delivery Semantics. Spacing around the dash is as rendered on the page.

claim: Many exactly-once claims are misleading once failures, multiple consumers or disk loss are considered.
quote: Many systems claim to provide “exactly-once” delivery semantics, but it is important to read the fine print, because sometimes these claims are misleading (i.e. they don’t translate to the case where consumers or producers can fail, cases where there are multiple consumer processes, or cases where data written to disk can be lost).

claim: A message is committed once all in-sync replicas have it; then it survives as long as one replica broker is alive.
quote: A message is considered committed only when all replicas in the in-sync replicas (ISR) for that partition have applied it to their log. Once a published message is committed, it will not be lost as long as one broker that replicates the partition to which this message was written remains “alive”.

claim: After a network error the producer cannot know whether the write happened, which is why retries create duplicates.
quote: If a producer attempts to publish a message and experiences a network error, it cannot be sure if this error happened before or after the message was committed. This is similar to the semantics of inserting into a database table with an autogenerated key.

claim: Since 0.11.0.0 the idempotent producer prevents duplicates from retries: broker-assigned producer ID plus a per-message sequence number.
quote: Since 0.11.0.0, the Kafka producer also supports an idempotent delivery option which guarantees that resending will not result in duplicate entries in the log. To achieve this, the broker assigns each producer an ID and deduplicates messages using a sequence number that is sent by the producer along with every message.

claim: Transactions let a producer write atomically to several partitions: all or nothing.
quote: Also beginning with 0.11.0.0, the producer supports the ability to send messages atomically to multiple topic partitions using transactions, so that either all messages are successfully written or none of them are.

claim: Waiting for a message to be committed takes on the order of 10 ms; producers can choose weaker durability for lower latency.
quote: If the producer specifies that it wants to wait on the message being committed, this can take on the order of 10 ms. However the producer can also specify that it wants to perform the send completely asynchronously or that it wants to wait only until the leader (but not necessarily the followers) have the message.

claim: Saving the position before processing gives at-most-once: a crash loses the unprocessed messages.
quote: It can read the messages, then save its position in the log, and finally process the messages. In this case there is a possibility that the consumer process crashes after saving its position but before saving the output of its message processing. In this case the process that took over processing would start at the saved position even though a few messages prior to that position had not been processed. This corresponds to “at-most-once” semantics as in the case of a consumer failure messages may not be processed.

claim: Processing before saving the position gives at-least-once: a crash causes reprocessing; idempotent updates make that harmless.
quote: It can read the messages, process the messages, and finally save its position. In this case there is a possibility that the consumer process crashes after processing messages but before saving its position. In this case when the new process takes over the first few messages it receives will already have been processed. This corresponds to the “at-least-once” semantics in the case of consumer failure. In many cases messages have a primary key and so the updates are idempotent (receiving the same message twice just overwrites a record with another copy of itself).

claim: Exactly-once for read-process-write: the consumer offset is written in the same transaction as the output; isolation level controls visibility; read_uncommitted is default.
quote: The consumer’s position is stored as a message in an internal topic, so we can write the offset to Kafka in the same transaction as the output topics receiving the processed data. If the transaction is aborted, the consumer’s stored position will revert to its old value (although the consumer has to refetch the committed offset because it does not automatically rewind) and the produced data on the output topics will not be visible to other consumers, depending on their “isolation level”. In the default “read_uncommitted” isolation level, all messages are visible to consumers even if they were part of an aborted transaction, but in “read_committed” isolation level, the consumer will only return messages from transactions which were committed (and any messages which were not part of a transaction).

claim: For external systems, store the offset in the same place as the output instead of two-phase commit.
quote: The classic way of achieving this would be to introduce a two-phase commit between the storage of the consumer position and the storage of the consumers output. This can be handled more simply and generally by letting the consumer store its offset in the same place as its output. This is better because many of the output systems a consumer might want to write to will not support a two-phase commit.

claim: Exactly-once is for Kafka-to-Kafka; other systems need cooperation; default is at-least-once; at-most-once by disabling retries and committing before processing.
quote: As a result, Kafka supports exactly-once delivery in Kafka Streams, and the transactional producer and the consumer using read-committed isolation level can be used generally to provide exactly-once delivery when reading, processing and writing data on Kafka topics. Exactly-once delivery for other destination systems generally requires cooperation with such systems, but Kafka provides the primitives which makes implementing this feasible (see also Kafka Connect). Otherwise, Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default, and allows the user to implement at-most-once delivery by disabling retries on the producer and committing offsets in the consumer prior to processing a batch of messages.

claim: Only the producer is transactional; it updates the consumer's committed offset inside the transaction.
quote: Kafka transactions are a bit different from transactions in other messaging systems. In Kafka, the consumer and producer are separate, and it is only the producer which is transactional. It is however able to make transactional updates to the consumer’s position (confusingly called the “committed offset”), and it is this which gives the overall exactly-once behavior.

claim: Exactly-once consumer needs read_committed and auto-commit off; producer needs transactional.id, which also aborts a previous instance's in-flight transaction.
quote: The consumer configuration must include isolation.level=read_committed and enable.auto.commit=false. The producer configuration must set transactional.id to the name of the transactional ID to be used, which configures the producer for transactional delivery and also makes sure that a restarted application causes any in-flight transaction from the previous instance to abort. Only the producer has the transactional.id configuration.

claim: Commit or abort writes transaction marker records; that is how read_committed consumers skip aborted records. The application must reset its position on abort.
quote: Any records written by the transactional producer will be marked as being part of the transactions, and then when the transaction commits or aborts, transaction marker records are written to indicate the outcome of the transaction. This is how the read-committed consumer does not see records from aborted transactions. However, in the event of a transaction abort, the application’s state and in particular the current position of the consumer must be reset explicitly so that it can reprocess the records processed by the aborted transaction.

claim: Share groups (queues for Kafka): many consumers per partition, more consumers than partitions, per-record acknowledgement, counted delivery attempts.
quote:
The consumers in a share group cooperatively consume records, and partitions may be assigned to multiple consumers.
The number of consumers in a share group can exceed the number of partitions in a topic.
Records are acknowledged individually, though the system is optimized for batch processing to improve efficiency.
Delivery attempts to consumers in a share group are counted, which enables automated handling of unprocessable records.
notes: Section The Share Consumer.

claim: Share consumers acquire records with a time-limited lock (30 s default) and can acknowledge, release, reject or renew.
quote:
By default, the lock duration is 30 seconds, but you can control it using the group configuration parameter share.record.lock.duration.ms. The lock is released automatically once its duration elapses, making the record available to another delivery attempt. A share consumer holding the lock can handle the record in the following ways:
Acknowledge successful processing of the record.
Release the record, making it available for another delivery attempt.
Reject the record, indicating it’s unprocessable and preventing further delivery attempts for that record.
Renew the record, extending the delivery attempt because the record is still being processed.
Do nothing, in which case the lock is automatically released when its duration elapses.
notes: Renew is listed in 4.3 docs; may be newer than 4.0/4.1.

claim: Topics are split into partitions; events with the same key go to the same partition; order is guaranteed within a partition.
quote: When a new event is published to a topic, it is actually appended to one of the topic’s partitions. Events with the same event key (e.g., a customer or vehicle ID) are written to the same partition, and Kafka guarantees that any consumer of a given topic-partition will always read that partition’s events in exactly the same order as they were written.
notes: The guarantee is per partition only; there is no cross-partition ordering.

claim: The producer chooses the partition, either randomly or by hashing a key; same user id means same partition.
quote: The client controls which partition it publishes messages to. This can be done at random, implementing a kind of random load balancing, or it can be done by some semantic partitioning function. We expose the interface for semantic partitioning by allowing the user to specify a key to partition by and using this to hash to a partition (there is also an option to override the partition function if need be). For example if the key chosen was a user id then all data for a given user would be sent to the same partition.

claim: Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a consumer group; the position is just one offset per partition.
quote: Our topic is divided into a set of totally ordered partitions, each of which is consumed by exactly one consumer within each subscribing consumer group at any given time. This means that the position of a consumer in each partition is just a single integer, the offset of the next message to consume. This makes the state about what has been consumed very small, just one number for each partition. This state can be periodically checkpointed. This makes the equivalent of message acknowledgements very cheap.

claim: Unlike traditional queues, events are not deleted when consumed; they are retained for a configured time per topic and can be reread.
quote: Events in a topic can be read as often as needed-unlike traditional messaging systems, events are not deleted after consumption. Instead, you define for how long Kafka should retain your events through a per-topic configuration setting, after which old events will be discarded. Kafka’s performance is effectively constant with respect to data size, so storing data for a long time is perfectly fine.

claim: Committed offsets are stored by the group coordinator in the compacted internal topic __consumer_offsets.
quote: When the group coordinator receives an OffsetCommitRequest, it appends the request to a special compacted Kafka topic named __consumer_offsets. The broker sends a successful offset commit response to the consumer only after all the replicas of the offsets topic receive the offsets.
notes: Section Consumer Offset Tracking; text verified from the single-page print view https://kafka.apache.org/43/_print/

claim: Producer acks default is all; acks=all waits for the full in-sync replica set; acks=1 can lose data if the leader fails right after acknowledging.
quote: acks=1 This will mean the leader will write the record to its local log but will respond without awaiting full acknowledgement from all followers. In this case should the leader fail immediately after acknowledging the record but before the followers have replicated it then the record will be lost.acks=all This means the leader will wait for the full set of in-sync replicas to acknowledge the record. This guarantees that the record will not be lost as long as at least one in-sync replica remains alive. This is the strongest available guarantee. This is equivalent to the acks=-1 setting.
notes: Config table shows Default:all. The change of default to all (and idempotence true) happened in Kafka 3.0 (KIP-679); see kafka_3_0_defaults entry.

claim: enable.idempotence defaults to true; it requires max.in.flight <= 5, retries > 0, acks=all; silently disabled if conflicting configs are set and it was not explicitly enabled.
quote: Note that enabling idempotence requires max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to be less than or equal to 5 (with message ordering preserved for any allowable value), retries to be greater than 0, and acks must be 'all'.Idempotence is enabled by default if no conflicting configurations are set. If conflicting configurations are set and idempotence is not explicitly enabled, idempotence is disabled.
notes: Default:true. Caveat for teaching: setting acks=1 quietly turns idempotence off.

claim: max.in.flight.requests.per.connection default is 5; with idempotence it must be at most 5 because the broker keeps only 5 batches per producer.
quote: Additionally, enabling idempotence requires the value of this configuration to be less than or equal to 5, because broker only retains at most 5 batches for each producer. If the value is more than 5, previous batches may be removed on broker side.
notes: Default:5

claim: delivery.timeout.ms default is 120000 ms (2 minutes): the upper bound for reporting success or failure of send().
quote: An upper bound on the time to report success or failure after a call to send() returns. This limits the total time that a record will be delayed prior to sending, the time to await acknowledgement from the broker (if expected), and the time allowed for retriable send failures.
notes: Default:120000 (2 minutes)

claim: Default linger.ms changed from 0 to 5 in Kafka 4.0.
quote: The default linger.ms changed from 0 to 5 in Apache Kafka 4.0 as the efficiency gains from larger batches typically result in similar or lower producer latency despite the increased linger.

claim: transaction.timeout.ms default is 60000 ms (1 minute); broker cap transaction.max.timeout.ms default 900000 ms (15 minutes).
quote: The maximum amount of time in milliseconds that a transaction will remain open before the coordinator proactively aborts it. The start of the transaction is set at the time that the first partition is added to it.
notes: Default:60000 (1 minute). Broker config transaction.max.timeout.ms Default:900000 (15 minutes) at https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/broker-configs/

claim: Consumer enable.auto.commit defaults to true, committing every auto.commit.interval.ms = 5000 ms in the background.
quote: If true the consumer's offset will be periodically committed in the background.
notes: Default:true. auto.commit.interval.ms: 'The frequency in milliseconds that the consumer offsets are auto-committed to Kafka if enable.auto.commit is set to true.' Default:5000 (5 seconds).

claim: max.poll.interval.ms default is 300000 ms (5 minutes); a consumer that does not poll in time is considered failed and its partitions are reassigned.
quote: The maximum delay between invocations of poll() when using consumer group management. This places an upper bound on the amount of time that the consumer can be idle before fetching more records. If poll() is not called before expiration of this timeout, then the consumer is considered failed and the group will rebalance in order to reassign the partitions to another member.
notes: Default:300000 (5 minutes)

claim: session.timeout.ms default is 45000 ms (45 s), heartbeat-based failure detection; under the new consumer protocol it is a broker setting instead.
quote: The timeout used to detect client failures when using Kafka's group management facility. The client sends periodic heartbeats to indicate its liveness to the broker. If no heartbeats are received by the broker before the expiration of this session timeout, then the broker will remove this client from the group and initiate a rebalance.
notes: Default:45000 (45 seconds). Not supported when group.protocol=consumer; then broker config group.consumer.session.timeout.ms applies.

claim: isolation.level default is read_uncommitted; read_committed returns only committed transactional messages, up to the last stable offset (LSO).
quote: If set to read_committed, consumer.poll() will only return transactional messages which have been committed. If set to read_uncommitted (the default), consumer.poll() will return all messages, even transactional messages which have been aborted. Non-transactional messages will be returned unconditionally in either mode.Messages will always be returned in offset order. Hence, in read_committed mode, consumer.poll() will only return messages up to the last stable offset (LSO), which is the one less than the offset of the first open transaction. In particular any messages appearing after messages belonging to ongoing transactions will be withheld until the relevant transaction has been completed.

claim: The consumer's group.protocol default is still classic in 4.3; the KIP-848 protocol is opt-in on the client with group.protocol=consumer.
quote: The group protocol that the consumer uses. The supported values are classic or consumer. The default value is classic.
notes: Surprise: KIP-848 is GA since 4.0 and enabled server-side, but clients still default to classic.

claim: Topic retention.ms default is 604800000 ms (7 days); it is an SLA on how soon consumers must read.
quote: This configuration controls the maximum time we will retain a log before we will discard old log segments to free up space if we are using the "delete" retention policy. This represents an SLA on how soon consumers must read their data. If set to -1, no time limit is applied.
notes: Default:604800000 (7 days). Broker log.retention.hours Default:168.

claim: Committed offsets of an empty group expire after offsets.retention.minutes, default 10080 (7 days).
quote: For subscribed consumers, committed offset of a specific partition will be expired and discarded when 1) this retention period has elapsed after the consumer group loses all its consumers (i.e. becomes empty); 2) this retention period has elapsed since the last time an offset is committed for the partition and the group is no longer subscribed to the corresponding topic.
notes: Default:10080 minutes

claim: KIP-848 next-generation consumer rebalance protocol is GA in Kafka 4.0.
quote: The Next Generation of the Consumer Rebalance Protocol (KIP-848) is now Generally Available (GA) in Apache Kafka 4.0. The protocol is automatically enabled on the server when the upgrade to 4.0 is finalized.

claim: KIP-890 Transactions Server-Side Defense ships in 4.0: the producer epoch is bumped on every transaction.
quote: Transactions Server-Side Defense (KIP-890) brings a strengthened transactional protocol to Apache Kafka 4.0. The new and improved transactional protocol is enabled when the upgrade to 4.0 is finalized. When using 4.0 producer clients, the producer epoch is bumped on every transaction to ensure every transaction includes the intended messages and duplicates are not written as part of the next transaction.

claim: Kafka 4.0 runs only in KRaft mode; ZooKeeper mode removed.
quote: Apache Kafka 4.0 only supports KRaft mode - ZooKeeper mode has been removed.
notes: Release date 18 March 2025 to be confirmed from the release blog (see kafka_4_0_release_date).

claim: Kafka 4.1 shipped Queues for Kafka (KIP-932) as a preview.
quote: Apache Kafka 4.1 ships with a preview of Queues for Kafka (KIP-932). This feature introduces a new kind of group called share groups, as an alternative to consumer groups. Consumers in a share group cooperatively consume records from topics, without assigning each partition to just one consumer. Share groups also introduce per-record acknowledgement and counting of delivery attempts. Use share groups in cases where records are processed one at a time, rather than as part of an ordered stream.

claim: Queues for Kafka (KIP-932) is production-ready in Kafka 4.2.
quote: Queues for Kafka (KIP-932) is production-ready in Apache Kafka 4.2. This feature introduces a new kind of group called share groups, as an alternative to consumer groups.
notes: Share group state lives in a new internal topic __share_group_state (same page).

claim: kafka-consumer-groups.sh shows each partition's committed offset, log end offset and LAG (how far behind the end of the log).
quote: We have a tool that will show the position of all consumers in a consumer group as well as how far behind the end of the log they are.
notes: Example output header: TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID HOST CLIENT-ID, with rows such as 'my-topic 0 2 4 2' (lag = log end offset minus current offset). Verified via https://kafka.apache.org/43/_print/. Monitoring metric records-lag-max: 'Number of messages the consumer lags behind the producer by. Published by the consumer, not broker.'

claim: Exactly-once with replication factor below 3 effectively voids EOS; use RF 3 with min.insync.replicas=2.
quote: While it is technically possible to use EOS with any replication factor, using a replication factor lower than 3 effectively voids EOS. Thus it is strongly recommended to use a replication factor of 3 (together with min.in.sync.replicas=2).
notes: From the Kafka Streams section of the 4.3 docs (single-page print view). 'min.in.sync.replicas' spelled as on the page.

claim: KIP-98 introduces a transaction coordinator per producer that assigns producer IDs and manages transactions.
quote: We introduce a new entity called a Transaction Coordinator. Similar to the consumer group coordinator, each producer is assigned a transaction coordinator, and all the logic of assigning PIDs and managing transactions is done by the transaction coordinator.
notes: KIP-98 status: Adopted (shipped in 0.11.0.0).

claim: The transaction log is an internal replicated topic holding the coordinator's state for every transaction.
quote: We introduce a new internal kafka topic called the Transaction Log. Similar to the Consumer Offsets topic, the transaction log is a persistent and replicated record of every transaction. The transaction log is the state store for the transaction coordinator, with the snapshot of the latest version of the log encapsulating the current state of each active transaction.
notes: The internal topic is named __transaction_state in the docs.

claim: Control messages (commit/abort markers) are written into user topics so consumers know whether fetched messages were committed.
quote: We introduce the notion of Control Messages. These are special messages written to user topics, processed by clients, but never exposed to users. They are used, for instance, to let brokers indicate to consumers if the previously fetched messages have been committed atomically or not. Control messages have been previously proposed here.

claim: The producer epoch ensures only one legitimate instance per transactional ID.
quote: We introduce the notion of a producer epoch, which enables us to ensure that there is only one legitimate active instance of a producer with a given TransactionalId, and hence enables us to maintain transaction guarantees in the event of failures.

claim: On init, the coordinator bumps the epoch so a previous zombie instance is fenced off.
quote: Bumps up the epoch of the PID, so that the any previous zombie instance of the producer is fenced off and cannot move forward with its transaction.

claim: sendOffsetsToTransaction adds the consumer group's offsets partition to the transaction (read-process-write).
quote: The sendOffsetsToTransaction method sends an AddOffsetCommitsToTxnRequests with the groupId to the transaction coordinator, from which it can deduce the TopicPartition for this consumer group in the internal __consumer-offsets topic. The transaction coordinator logs the addition of this topic partition to the transaction log in step 4.3a.
notes: The KIP text writes __consumer-offsets with a hyphen; the actual topic is __consumer_offsets.

claim: At commit, the coordinator has each partition leader write a COMMIT or ABORT control marker.
quote: This request is issued by the transaction coordinator to the the leader of each TopicPartition which is part of the transaction. Upon receiving this request, each broker will write a COMMIT(PID) or ABORT(PID) control message to the log. (step 5.2a)

claim: A transactional ID permits one active producer; zombies are fenced by an epoch.
quote: In Kafka EOS, we use the concept of a "transactional Id" in order to preserve exactly once processing guarantees across process failures and restarts. Essentially this allows us to guarantee that for a given transactional Id, there can only be one producer instance that is active and permitted to make progress at any time. Zombie producers are fenced by an epoch which is associated with each transactional Id. We can also guarantee that upon initialization, any transactions which were still in progress are completed before we begin processing. This is the point of the initTransactions() API.
notes: KIP-447 status: Adopted (2.6.0).

claim: KIP-447 problem: consumer-group partition ownership moves on rebalance, but transactional IDs assumed static assignment, forcing one producer per input partition.
quote: The problem we are trying to solve in this proposal is a semantic mismatch between consumers in a group and transactional producers. In a consumer group, ownership of partitions can transfer between group members through the rebalance protocol. For transactional producers, assignments are assumed to be static. Every transactional id must map to a consistent set of input partitions. To preserve the static partition mapping in a consumer group where assignments are frequently changing, the simplest solution is to create a separate producer for every input partition. This is what Kafka Streams does today.
notes: Fix: sendOffsetsToTransaction takes ConsumerGroupMetadata so the group coordinator fences zombies by generation; Adopted in 2.6.0.

claim: KIP-447 changes sendOffsetsToTransaction to take consumer group metadata.
quote: void sendOffsetsToTransaction(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> offsets, ConsumerGroupMetadata consumerGroupMetadata) throws ProducerFencedException, FencedInstanceIdException; // NEW
notes: The older overload taking a String groupId was removed in 4.0 per the upgrade notes.

claim: KIP-890 addresses hanging transactions: the LSO stops advancing, compaction stalls, read_committed consumers get stuck.
quote: We have seen hanging transactions in Kafka where the last stable offset (LSO) does not update, we can’t clean the log (if the topic is compacted), and read_committed consumers get stuck.
notes: Shipped in Kafka 4.0 (upgrade notes); KIP status shows Approved.

claim: A delayed message from an aborted transaction can end up in the next transaction, violating EOS.
quote: This can happen when a message gets stuck or delayed due to networking issues or a network partition, the transaction aborts, and then the delayed message finally comes in. The delayed message case can also violate EOS if the delayed message comes in after the next addPartitionsToTxn request comes in. Effectively we may see a message from a previous (aborted) transaction become part of the next transaction. A similar event can occur if a delayed EndTxn marker comes through an a new transaction with the same epoch has started when the request is received. This can result in incorrectly completing a transaction.

claim: KIP-890 fix: bump the producer epoch after every commit or abort so each transaction is identified by (producer id, epoch).
quote: Uniquely identify transactions by bumping the producer epoch after every commit/abort marker. That way, each transaction can be identified by (producer id, epoch).

claim: Kafka 4.0 released 18 March 2025: first major release to run entirely without ZooKeeper (KRaft by default).
quote: Apache Kafka 4.0 is a significant milestone, marking the first major release to operate entirely without Apache ZooKeeper®.
notes: Post by David Jacot, dated Tuesday, March 18, 2025.

claim: KIP-848 GA in 4.0 ends stop-the-world rebalances; enabled by default on the server; consumers must opt in with group.protocol=consumer.
quote: Apache Kafka says goodbye to “stop-the-world” rebalances with the general availability of the next generation of the consumer rebalance protocol. It increases the stability and the performance of consumer groups while simplifying clients. The new protocol is enabled by default on the server side. Consumers must opt-in by setting group.protocol=consumer.

claim: 4.0 completed phase two of KIP-890, reducing zombie transactions.
quote: The second phase of KIP-890 has been completed. It reduces the chances of “zombie transactions” during producer failures.

claim: Queues for Kafka (share groups) was early access in 4.0; it adds cooperative consumption on regular topics, not a new queue object.
quote: This KIP introduces the concept of a share group as a way of enabling cooperative consumption using Kafka topics. It does not add the concept of a “queue” to Kafka per se, but rather introduces cooperative consumption to accommodate these queuing use-cases, using regular Kafka topics. Share groups make this possible. You can think of a share group as roughly equivalent to a “durable shared subscription” in existing systems.
notes: Heading on page: KIP-932: Queues for Kafka (Early Access).

claim: In 4.1 Queues for Kafka is a preview, not production ready.
quote: Queues for Kafka (KIP-932) is now in preview. It’s still not ready for production but you can start evaluating and testing it.

claim: In 4.2 share groups are production ready, adding RENEW acknowledgement and lag metrics.
quote: Kafka Queues (Share Groups) is now production-ready with new features like the RENEW acknowledgement type for extended processing times, adaptive batching for share coordinators, soft and strict enforcements of quantity of fetched records, and comprehensive lag metrics.
notes: The kafka-site repo also has a 2026/01/14 path for the 4.2.0 announcement that redirects to the 2026/02/17 post. Kafka 4.3.0 was announced 2026-05-22 (latest minor at fetch time; 4.3.1 on 2026-06-25).

claim: Since Kafka 3.0 the producer defaults to idempotence on and acks=all (was acks=1); a bug kept idempotence off in 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 until 3.0.1/3.1.1/3.2.0.
quote: The producer has stronger delivery guarantees by default: idempotence is enabled and acks is set to all instead of 1. See KIP-679 for details. In 3.0.0 and 3.1.0, a bug prevented the idempotence default from being applied which meant that it remained disabled unless the user had explicitly set enable.idempotence to true. Note that the bug did not affect the acks=all change. See KAFKA-13598for more details. This issue was fixed and the default is properly applied in 3.0.1, 3.1.1, and 3.2.0.
notes: Upgrade notes for 3.0.0, KIP-679. Bug: KAFKA-13598.

claim: Before 3.0 the producer defaulted to at-least-once with enable.idempotence=false.
quote: Exactly Once Delivery. In KIP-98, the community introduces Exactly Once Delivery, which guarantees that every message will be persisted exactly once without data loss or duplication. However, in order to give the community time for upgrading, by default, the producer will still use at-least-once delivery and set "enable.idempotence=false".
notes: KIP-679 Current state: APPROVED.

claim: Exactly-once needs cooperation between the messaging system and the application; rewinding a consumer replays messages.
quote: Exactly-once semantics is the most desirable guarantee, but also a poorly understood one. This is because it requires a cooperation between the messaging system itself and the application producing and consuming the messages. For instance, if after consuming a message successfully you rewind your Kafka consumer to a previous offset, you will receive all the messages from that offset to the latest one, all over again.
notes: Neha Narkhede; page says originally published 2017 and last updated March 2025.

claim: At-least-once: if the broker writes the message but fails before acking, the producer's retry writes it twice.
quote: If the broker had failed right before it sent the ack but after the message was successfully written to the Kafka topic, this retry leads to the message being written twice and hence delivered more than once to the end consumer.

claim: Idempotent producer works like TCP sequence numbers but persisted in the replicated log, with negligible overhead.
quote: Under the covers, it works in a way similar to TCP: each batch of messages sent to Kafka will contain a sequence number that the broker will use to dedupe any duplicate send. Unlike TCP, though—which provides guarantees only within a transient in-memory connection—this sequence number is persisted to the replicated log, so even if the leader fails, any broker that takes over will also know if a resend is a duplicate. The overhead of this mechanism is quite low: it’s just a few extra numeric fields with each batch of messages.
notes: Quote contains an em-dash from the source; paraphrase on the page if needed (house style forbids em-dashes).

claim: Measured overhead (2017): transactional producer with 1 KB messages and 100 ms transactions loses 3% throughput vs at-least-once in-order, 20% vs at-most-once acks=1.
quote: For 1 KB messages and transactions lasting 100 ms, the producer throughput declines only by 3%, compared to the throughput of a producer configured for at least once, in-order delivery (acks=all, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1), and by 20% compared to the throughput of a producer configured for most once delivery with no ordering guarantees (acks=1, max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5), which is the current default.
notes: 'current default' refers to 2017 (acks=1); defaults changed in 3.0.

claim: Exactly-once in Kafka Streams with a 100 ms commit interval cost 15% to 30% throughput (2017); a 30 s interval had no overhead for messages of 1 KB or more.
quote: We also had a look into the overhead of exactly-once stream processing using the Streams API. With a short commit interval of 100 ms—that is required to keep end-to-end latency low—we see a throughput degradation of 15% to 30% depending on the message size, which is a 1 KB message size for the former and 100 bytes for the latter. However, a larger commit interval of 30 seconds has no overhead at all for larger message sizes of 1 KB or higher.
notes: Quote contains an em-dash from the source; paraphrase on the page (house style forbids em-dashes).

claim: A Kinesis Data Streams shard supports writes of 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s and reads of 2 MB/s.
quote: Each shard can support up to 5 transactions per second for reads, up to a maximum total data read rate of 2 MB per second and up to 1,000 records per second for writes, up to a maximum total data write rate of 1 MB per second (including partition keys).
notes: Provisioned mode. The quotas page phrases it: 'Each shard can support up to 1 MB/sec or 1,000 records/sec write throughput or up to 2 MB/sec or 2,000 records/sec read throughput.' (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/service-sizes-and-limits.html). Max record (data blob) 1 MB.

claim: Kinesis keeps records 24 hours by default, extendable to 365 days.
quote: A Kinesis data stream stores records from 24 hours by default, up to 8760 hours (365 days).
notes: Retention above 24 hours costs extra.

claim: Redpanda is a transaction log for event streams that clients talk to with the Kafka API; each partition is a Raft group.
quote: At its core, Redpanda is a fault-tolerant transaction log for storing event streams. Producers and consumers interact with Redpanda using the Kafka API.
notes: Same page: 'Every topic partition forms a Raft group consisting of a single elected leader and zero or more followers'.

claim: Redpanda is built in C++ and ships as a single binary with no external dependencies (no ZooKeeper).
quote:
Built on C++, Redpanda delivers greater throughput and up to 10x lower p99 latencies than other platforms. This enables previously unimaginable use cases that require high throughput, low latency, and a minimal hardware footprint.
Redpanda is packaged as a single binary: it doesn’t rely on any external systems.
notes: 10x latency claim is vendor marketing. The page does not name ZooKeeper; 'doesn't rely on any external systems' is the supporting line.

claim: Apache Pulsar: multi-tenant messaging from Yahoo, storage in Apache BookKeeper, tiered storage.
quote: Pulsar is a multi-tenant, high-performance solution for server-to-server messaging. Originally developed by Yahoo, Pulsar is under the stewardship of the Apache Software Foundation.
notes: Same page: 'Guaranteed message delivery with persistent message storage provided by Apache BookKeeper.'

claim: Jepsen's Bufstream 0.1.0 report also found Kafka-wide problems: undocumented transaction semantics, a Java client deadlock, and write loss / aborted reads / torn transactions from the transaction protocol.
quote: We also characterize four issues related to Kafka more generally, including the lack of authoritative documentation for transaction semantics, a deadlock in the official Java client, and write loss, aborted read, and torn transactions caused by the lack of message ordering constraints in the Kafka transaction protocol. These issues affect Kafka, Bufstream, and (presumably) other Kafka-compatible systems, and remain unresolved.
notes: 'remain unresolved' as of the report date.

claim: Root cause: Kafka's transaction protocol has no sequence or transaction number, so a commit may apply to whatever transaction is in progress.
quote: This suggests a fundamental problem in the Kafka transaction protocol. The protocol is designed to allow clients to submit requests over multiple TCP connections and to distribute them across multiple nodes. There is no sequence number to order requests from the same client. There is no concept of a transaction number. When a server receives a commit (or abort) message, it has no way to know what transaction the client intended to commit. It simply commits (or aborts) whatever transaction happens to be in progress.
notes: A footnote marker '12' after 'transaction number.' on the page has been removed from the quote.

claim: Jepsen reproduced aborted reads and torn transactions in Kafka itself (KAFKA-17754); Kafka engineers expected KIP-890 (epoch bump per transaction) to fix it.
quote: We observed aborted reads and torn transactions due to process pauses in Kafka as well, and opened KAFKA-17754 to track the issue. Kafka’s engineers believe KIP-890, which was motivated by hanging transactions in Kafka, will likely fix the problem. In brief, KIP-890 revises the transaction protocol to bump the producer’s epoch on every transaction. Since servers reject messages from older epochs, this should prevent commit messages from prior transactions leaking into later ones. KIP-890 was opened in November 2022, and work is ongoing.
notes: KIP-890 phase two later shipped in Kafka 4.0 (March 2025); whether KAFKA-17754 is fully closed was not checked.

claim: After a transaction abort the consumer does not rewind automatically; the application must seek back (KAFKA-17582, intended behaviour).
quote: Consumers continue advancing, unless they happen to be rebalanced, in which case they might rewind to an arbitrary point—whatever happens to be committed. Users are supposed to manually rewind the consumer’s position on transaction abort.
notes: Contains an em-dash from the source.

claim: Auto-commit semantics are murky: the Java client commits offsets of the penultimate poll, not the latest; Jepsen withdrew its auto-commit data-loss claim.
quote: However, several readers objected that auto-commit consumers do not in fact commit the offsets of the most recent poll. Rather, they commit the offsets of the penultimate poll—the poll before the most recent poll. Brief experiments with the Java Kafka client appear to support this claim. To further complicate matters, Buf indicates that some clients commit offsets of the penultimate poll, and other clients use the most recent poll. We have removed specific claims regarding auto-commit from this report; more research is warranted.
notes: Erratum dated 2024-11-13. Useful caveat: do not teach that auto-commit loses data by default without qualification. Quote contains an em-dash from the source; paraphrase on the page (house style forbids em-dashes).

claim: Jepsen found seven safety issues in Redpanda 21.10.1, including aborted reads and lost/stale messages, plus confusing docs about Kafka's transaction isolation.
quote: We found three liveness and seven safety issues, ranging from crashes and aborted reads to inconsistent offsets, circular information flow, and lost/stale messages. We also discuss some potentially surprising behaviors, including an ambiguously named error and confusing documentation around write isolation in Kafka’s transaction model. Redpanda has resolved seven of these issues, though some fixes aren’t yet released.
notes: Same report: Redpanda 'uses the Raft consensus algorithm internally, rather than depending on a separate installation of Zookeeper.'

claim: NATS JetStream 2.12.1 acknowledges writes immediately but fsyncs only every two minutes by default, so acknowledged writes can be lost.
quote: NATS JetStream promises that once a publish call has been acknowledged, it is “successfully persisted”. This is not exactly true. By default, NATS calls fsync to flush data to disk only once every two minutes, but acknowledges messages immediately. Consequently, recently acknowledged writes are generally not persisted, and could be lost to coordinated power failure, kernel crashes, etc. For instance, simulated power failures in this test run caused NATS to lose roughly thirty seconds of writes:
notes: Abstract: 'This data loss was caused (at least in part) by choosing to flush writes to disk every two minutes, rather than before acknowledging them.'

claim: Peak throughput: Kafka 605 MB/s, Pulsar 305 MB/s, RabbitMQ (mirrored) 38 MB/s. p99 latency: Kafka 5 ms and Pulsar 25 ms at 200 MB/s; RabbitMQ 1 ms only at a reduced 30 MB/s load.
quote:
Peak Throughput(MB/s)
605MB/s
305MB/s
38MB/s
p99 Latency(ms)
5 ms(200 MB/s load)
25 ms(200 MB/s load)
1 ms*(reduced 30 MB/s load)
*RabbitMQ latencies degrade significantly at throughputs higher than the 30 MB/s. Furthermore, the impact of mirroring is significant at higher throughput and better latencies can be achieved by using just classic queues without mirroring.
notes: Confluent vendor benchmark (Alok Nikhil, Vinoth Chandar), dated Aug 21, 2020. The page's current title reads 'Benchmarking Apache Pulsar, Kafka, and RabbitMQ'; the original title was 'Benchmarking Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, and RabbitMQ: Which is the Fastest?'. Table columns are Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ(Mirrored), in that order; text is flattened from the HTML table.

claim: Testbed: three broker instances of AWS i3en.2xlarge (8 vCores, 64 GB RAM, 2 x 2,500 GB NVMe SSD, 25 Gbps), about 655 MB/s disk write ceiling; four worker instances.
quote: All tests deploy four worker instances to drive workload, three broker/server instances, one monitoring instance, and optionally a three-instance Apache ZooKeeper cluster for Kafka and Pulsar.
notes: Same page: 'we went with the i3en.2xlarge (with 8 vCores, 64 GB RAM, 2 x 2,500 GB NVMe SSDs) for its high 25 Gbps network transfer limit ... i3en.2xlarge instances support up to ~655 MB/s of write throughput across two disks'.

claim: RabbitMQ (mirrored queues) was CPU bound at about 38K msgs/s with p99 near two seconds; at 30K msgs/s p99 was 1 ms.
quote: Due to CPU bottlenecks, we were not able to drive a throughput higher than 38K messages/s, and any attempt to measure latency at this rate showed significant degradation in performance clocking a p99 latency of almost two seconds.
notes: Next paragraph: lowering to 30K messages/s 'was confirmed by a significantly better p99 latency of 1 ms.' Messages were 1 KB.

claim: Latency test conditions: 1 ms batching, Kafka with default fsync off, RabbitMQ not persisting messages but mirroring; Kafka and Pulsar compared at 200K msgs/s (200 MB/s).
quote: Kafka was configured to use its default fsync settings (i.e., fsync off), and RabbitMQ was configured to not persist messages while still mirroring the queues. Based on repeated runs, we chose to compare Kafka and Pulsar at 200K messages/s or 200MB/s, which is below the single disk throughput limit of 300 MB/s on this testbed.
notes: Important caveat for teaching: Kafka's default does not fsync each message; durability comes from replication.

claim: RabbitMQ queues do not support rewinding to reread old messages, unlike Kafka and Pulsar (as of 2020).
quote: RabbitMQ operates with a durable queue that persists messages to the disk if and only if the messages have not already been consumed. Unlike Kafka and Pulsar, however, RabbitMQ does not support ‘rewinding’ of queues to read older messages yet again.
notes: Out of date: RabbitMQ Streams (3.9, 2021) are replayable logs.
